references.text: Deuteronomy expands the law about helping an enemy's animal to include all situations where one finds lost animals or sees them collapse under their burden, and imposes a duty to help.
Proverbs teaches showing kindness to enemies by giving them food and drink, reflecting the principle of helping one's enemy as in Exodus 23:4.
Jesus teaches to love one's enemies and pray for those who persecute you, which expands on the Old Testament command to help an enemy's animal.
Paul quotes Proverbs and urges believers to overcome evil with good, including showing kindness to enemies.
The command to love your neighbor as yourself forms the basis for helping even an enemy's property.
Deuteronomy expands and confirms the law about returning stray animals from Exodus.
Deuteronomy provides the necessary procedure for cases where the owner of the stray animal is not immediately known.
Leviticus anchors the ethical duty to return found property (as in Exodus) within the framework of guilt offerings and restoration.
